#Text=Then they made a plan that the next day the mother
#Text= should take the plough afield, while Anuwa should dress up as an old
#Text= woman and carry the breakfast.
#Text=This they did and the jackal met Anuwa
#Text= as usual and made him put down the breakfast basket, but while the
#Text= jackal was eating, Anuwa knocked him head over heels with his stick;
#Text= and the jackal got up and fled, threatening and cursing Anuwa.
#Text=Among
#Text= other things the jackal as he ran away, had threatened to eat Anuwa  '  s
#Text= _malhan_ plants, so Anuwa put a fence of thorns round them and when
#Text= the jackal came at night and tried to eat the pods he only got his
#Text= nose pricked.
#Text=Foiled in this the jackal called out "Well, I will eat your fowls
#Text= to-morrow;" but Anuwa the next night sat by the fowl house with a
#Text= sickle and when the jackal came and poked in his head, Anuwa gave him a
#Text= rap on the snout with the sickle, so the jackal made off crying "Well,
#Text= Anuwa, your fowls have pecked me on the head, you shall die."
#Text=So the
#Text= next day Anuwa pretended to be dead and his mother went about crying;
#Text= she took her way to the jungle and there she met the jackal and she
#Text= told him that Anuwa had died in consequence of his curse and she
#Text= invited him to the funeral feast, saying that he used to eat the
#Text="Ho, leopard: Ho, leopard," and the echo used to answer from the hill
#Text= "Ho, leopard."
#Text=Now there really was a leopard who lived in the hill
#Text= and one day he was playing hide and seek with a lizard which also
#Text= lived there.
#Text=The lizard hid and the leopard looked every where for
#Text= it in vain.
#Text=At last the leopard sat down to rest and it chanced that
#Text= he sat right on top of the lizard which was hiding in a hole.
#Text=The
#Text= lizard thought that the leopard meant to hurt it and in revenge bit
#Text= him and fastened on to his rump so that he could not get it off,
#Text= so that day when the boys came calling out "Ho, leopard," he ran
#Text= towards them to get their help: but when they saw the leopard they
#Text= all fled for their lives.
#Text=Ledha however could not run fast because
#Text= he was lame, and the leopard headed him off and begged him to remove
#Text= the lizard.
#Text=This he did after the leopard had sworn not to eat him,
#Text= and before they parted the leopard made him promise to tell no one
#Text= that the lizard had bitten him, and said that if he told then he would
#Text= be carried off and eaten.
#Text=So Ledha rejoined his companions and told
#Text= them nothing of what had passed between him and the leopard.
#Text=But that
#Text= night when they had all gone to bed, Ledha  '  s sister-in-law began to
#Text= worry him to tell her what the leopard had said to him, when it had
#Text= caught him.
#Text=He told her that the leopard would eat him if he told,
#Text=but she coaxed him and said that no one could hear them inside the
#Text= house; so at last he told her that he had taken off a lizard which
#Text= was hanging on to its rump.
#Text=Then they went to sleep; but the leopard
#Text= was hiding at the back of the house and heard all that they said;
#Text= and when they were all asleep, he crept in and carried off Ledha  '  s bed
#Text= with Ledha in it on his head.
#Text=When Ledha woke up towards morning, he
#Text= found himself being carried through dense jungle and he quietly pulled
#Text= himself up into one of the trees which overhung the path.
#Text=Thus when
#Text= the leopard put down the bed and was going to eat Ledha, he found it
#Text= empty.
#Text=So he went back on his track and by and bye came to the tree
#Text= in which Ledha was hiding.
#Text=The leopard begged Ledha to come down,
#Text= as he had something to say to him, and promised not to eat him; but
#Text= directly Ledha reached the ground the leopard said "Now I am going to
#Text= eat you."
#Text=Ledha was powerless, so he only asked to be allowed to have
#Text= one chew of tobacco before he died; the leopard assented and Ledha
#Text= felt in his cloth for his tobacco, but the tobacco did not come out
#Text= easily and as Ledha felt about for it the dry tobacco leaves crackled;
#Text= the leopard asked what the crackling sound was, and Ledha said "That
#Text= is the lizard which bit you yesterday;" then the leopard got into a

#Text=The Ghormuhas could run
#Text= very fast and they made Somai run a race with them every day and
#Text= their plan was that they would eat him when he was strong enough to
#Text= beat them in the race.
#Text=In the course of time he came to beat them in
#Text= running on the road; then they said that they would make him run in
#Text= the fields and, if he beat them there, they meant to eat him.
#Text=Jogi came to the palace begging, and the Raja and his Ranis asked him
#Text= whether he could say what should be done in order that they might
#Text= have children; the Jogi asked what they would give him if he told
#Text= them and they said that they would give him anything that he asked
#Text= for and gave him a written bond to this effect.
#Text=Then the Jogi said
#Text= "I will not take elephants or horses or money, but you shall give me
#Text= the child which is born first and any born afterwards shall be yours,
#Text= do you agree?"
#Text=And the Ranis consulted together and agreed.
#Text="Then,"
#Text= said the Jogi, "this is what you must do: you must all go and bathe,
#Text= and after bathing you must go to a mango orchard and the Raja must
#Text= choose a bunch of seven mangoes and knock it down with his left
#Text= hand and catch it in a cloth, without letting it touch the ground;
#Text= then you must go home and the Ranis must sit in a row according to
#Text= their seniority and the Raja must give them each one of the mangoes
#Text= to eat, and he must himself eat the rinds which the Ranis throw away;
#Text= and then you will have children."
#Text=And so saying the Jogi went away
#Text= promising to return the next year.

column1: #Text= cow: "the tree is right, see how men treat cattle; you drive away our
#Text= calves from us and take our milk and you beat us and make us work hard;
#Text= for all this ill treatment the snake shall eat you."
#Text=Then the prince asked the water what it had to say: "I agree with the
#Text= other two" said the water: "to return evil for good is the justice of
#Text= mankind, it is by drinking water that your very lives are preserved;
#Text= yet you spit into it and wash dirty things in it; shall not the snake
#Text= return you evil for good?"
#Text=So judgment was delivered, and the snake
#Text= wanted to eat the prince; but the prince asked the tree and the cow
#Text= and the water to listen while he made one prayer; he told them how
#Text= he had been married when he was too young to know anything about it,
#Text= and how he was going for the first time to see his wife, when this
#Text= misfortune befell him; so he begged that he might be allowed to go and
#Text= see his bride and then be eaten on his way back; the banyan tree asked
#Text=
#Text= The next morning came and the prince said that he must return, and
#Text= his wife said that she was going with him; so they made everything
#Text= ready and set out on their way.
#Text=When they came within sight of the
#Text= banyan tree where the prince was to be killed, he tried to turn his
#Text= wife back but though he used force she refused to leave him and said
#Text= that she would first see him killed and then go home; so at last he
#Text= let her accompany him.
#Text=When they reached the tree she asked to be allowed to go in front and
#Text= be the first to meet the snake; to this the prince assented.
#Text=They
#Text= had not gone far when they saw the snake awaiting them in the path
#Text= with its crest raised, and when they drew near, the prince  '  s bride
#Text= begged the snake to eat her first, as she had nowhere to live if she
#Text= survived her husband.
#Text=The snake refused and bade her go home to her
#Text= parents; she said that that was impossible; they had sold her and the
#Text= prince had bought her, in life and in death, bones and ashes.
#Text=But
#Text= the snake would not listen and made for the prince to eat him.
#Text=His
#Text= wife however kept in front of the snake and would not let it pass;
#Text= she called the banyan tree to witness that the snake should not eat
#Text=and ran off with her on his back.
#Text=The girl was quite willing to go with him and called out as she was
#Text= carried away: "Never mind, father and mother, I am going away."
#Text=The
#Text= Hanuman took her to a cave in the mountains and they lived on
#Text= fruit,--mangoes or jack or whatever fruit was in season.
#Text=The monkey
#Text= climbed the trees and shook the fruit down; but if the girl saw by
#Text= the marks of teeth that the monkey had bitten off any fruit, instead
#Text= of only shaking it down, she would not eat it, and pretended that
#Text= she had had enough; for she would not eat the leavings of the monkey.
#Text=At last the girl got tired of having only fruit to eat; and demanded
#Text= rice.
#Text=So the monkey took her to a bazar, and leaving her on the
#Text= outskirts of the village under a tree, he went and stole some pots from
#Text= a potter and rice and salt and turmeric and pulse and sweetmeats from
#Text= other shops, and brought them to the girl.
#Text=Then she collected sticks
#Text= and lit a fire and cooked a meal; and the monkey liked the cooked
#Text= food, and asked her to cook for him every day.
#Text=So they stayed there
#Text= several days.
#Text=Then the girl asked for more clothes and the monkey
#Text= tried to steal them too, but the shopkeepers were on the watch and
#Text=When the leopard heard the shouting and the drumming, it started to
#Text= escape to another jungle, and as it was crossing a road it came on
#Text= a merchant driving a packbullock.
#Text=The merchant tried to run away,
#Text= but the leopard stopped him and said "You must hide me or I will eat
#Text= you."
#Text=The merchant continued to run, thinking that if he helped the
#Text= leopard it would surely eat him afterwards, but the leopard swore an
#Text= oath not to eat him if he would only hide it.
#Text=So the merchant stopped
#Text= and took one of his sacks off the bullock and emptied it out and tied
#Text= up the leopard in it, and put it on the bullock and then drove on.
#Text=When they got out of hearing of the hunters the leopard asked to be
#Text= let out; but directly the sack was untied it said that it would devour
#Text= the merchant.
#Text=The merchant said "You can of course eat me, but let us
#Text= consult an arbitrator as to whether it is fair."
#Text=The leopard agreed
#Text= and as they were near a stream, the man asked the water whether it was
#Text= fair that he should be killed, after he had saved the leopard  '  s life;
#Text= the water answered "Yes; you men wash all manner of filthy things
#Text= in me; let it eat you!"
#Text=Then the leopard wanted to eat him, but the
#Text= merchant asked leave to take two more opinions; so he asked a tree;
#Text= but the tree said "Men cut me down; let the leopard eat you."

#Text=The Coldest Season.
#Text=One winter day a bear and a tiger began to dispute as to which is
#Text= the coldest season of the year; the bear said July and August, which
#Text= is the rainy season, and the tiger said December and January, which
#Text= is the winter season.
#Text=They argued and argued but could not convince
#Text= each other; for the bear with his long coat did not feel the cold of
#Text= winter but when he got soaked through in the rain he felt chilly.
#Text=At last they saw a man coming that way and called on him to
#Text= decide--"but have a care"--said the tiger--"if you give an opinion
#Text= favourable to the bear, I will eat you;" and the bear said "If you
#Text= side with the tiger, _I_ will eat you."
#Text=At this the man was terror
#Text= stricken but an idea struck him and he made the tiger and the bear
#Text= promise not to eat him if he gave a fair decision and then he said
#Text= "It is not the winter which is the coldest, nor the rainy season which
#Text= is the coldest, but windy weather; if there is no wind no one feels
#Text= the cold much either in the winter or in the rainy season."
#Text=And the
#Text= tiger and the bear said "You are right, we never thought of that"

#Text=(2)--The Sons of the Tigress.
#Text=Once upon a time a cow and a tigress lived in a jungle and were great
#Text= friends, they were never separated.
#Text=Now in those days tigers did not
#Text= eat flesh, but grazed like cattle, so the tigress never thought of
#Text= doing any harm to her friend the cow.
#Text=The tigress had given birth
#Text= to two men children who were growing up fine and sturdy lads.
#Text=One
#Text= afternoon the cow and the tigress went down to a stream to drink,
#Text= the cow went into the stream and drank and the tigress drank lower
#Text= down.
#Text=The cow fouled the water of the stream and the tigress tasting
#Text= the water found it sweet and thought if the cow can make the water so
#Text= sweet how sweet the flesh of the cow must be.
#Text=So on the way back from
#Text= the stream the tigress suddenly sprang on the cow and killed her and
#Text=their return.
#Text=One day while the brothers were hunting the girl went to cut herbs
#Text= to cook with the dinner: as she was doing so she chanced to cut her
#Text= finger and some drops of blood fell on the herbs, which were put in
#Text= the pot.
#Text=When the brothers came home to dinner they noticed how very
#Text= sweet the food was and asked the reason.
#Text=The girl said that she was
#Text= afraid that it must be because some drops of her blood had fallen
#Text= on it.
#Text=Then the brothers took counsel together and agreed that if
#Text= a few drops of her blood were so sweet, she must be very nice to
#Text= eat.
#Text=So they agreed to murder her and eat her.
#Text=But the youngest
#Text= brother named Lita, though he did not dare to oppose his elders,
#Text= was sorry for the decision.
#Text=The next day when the brothers came
#Text= from the jungle they brought with them a beautiful flower of seven
#Text= colours and gave it to their sister.
#Text=She was delighted with it:
#Text= she had never seen so beautiful a flower before and wanted to know
#Text= where it grew and whether were others like it.
#Text=They said that if she
#Text= liked to come with them they would take her to the tree on which the
#Text= flowers grew and she could pick as many as she liked.
